title: Campaign Finance Superpacs
headline: Campaign Finance Superpacs
question: How did “money is speech” go from a 1971 think tank paper to billion-dollar campaigns?
intro: In 1971 a Yale law professor writing for the American Enterprise Institute argued that spending money on politics is speech. Over the next 39 years the courts agreed, one case at a time, until 2010 gave us the super PAC. Move the idea through the people who carried it, and watch what presidential campaigns spent.

stations.title: Keep corporate money out
stations.what: Bans corporate contributions to federal campaigns.
stations.pitch: Corporate money corrupts elections, so keep it out of them.
stations.spread: The first federal limit. Later laws build on it for most of the century.

stations.title: Unions too
stations.what: Bans union contributions and restricts corporate and union spending on federal elections.
stations.pitch: Neither unions nor corporations should spend on federal elections.
stations.spread: Restrictions on corporate and union election spending hold, in one form or another, until 2010.

stations.title: Business, get organized
stations.where: A memo for the U.S. Chamber of Commerce
stations.what: “Attack on the American Free Enterprise System” urges business to organize politically and in the courts.
stations.pitch: Business should fight for its interests in politics and in court.
stations.spread: Powell is nominated to the Supreme Court later that year. Critics see the memo behind his 1978 Bellotti opinion; that link is their interpretation.

stations.title: Money is speech
stations.who: Ralph K. Winter Jr., Yale Law School, with John R. Bolton
stations.where: American Enterprise Institute, papers of 1971 and 1973
stations.what: “Money, Politics and the First Amendment” (1971) and Campaign Financing and Political Freedom (1973), written against the limits Congress was passing.
stations.pitch: A limit on campaign money is a limit on political speech.
stations.spread: Winter takes the argument to court as lead lawyer in Buckley. Bolton later calls him the intellectual father of the arguments the Court accepted.

stations.title: Cap the money
stations.where: The Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 and its 1974 amendments
stations.what: Caps gifts at $1,000 per person and $5,000 per committee for each election, limits spending, and creates the Federal Election Commission.
stations.pitch: After Watergate, put a ceiling on campaign money.
stations.spread: Ford signs the amendments on October 15, 1974. The lawsuit against them is filed on January 2, 1975.

stations.title: The Court agrees, halfway
stations.who: Sen. James Buckley, Eugene McCarthy, donor Stewart Mott and a left-right coalition
stations.where: Supreme Court, argued by Ralph Winter
stations.what: Limits on spending are struck down; limits on contributions to candidates and disclosure survive.
stations.pitch: Spending money on elections is political speech.
stations.spread: The plaintiffs ran from the American Conservative Union to the Socialist Workers Party. Every later campaign finance case builds on this one.

stations.title: Corporations can speak
stations.where: First National Bank of Boston v. Bellotti
stations.what: Corporations may spend money on ballot questions.
stations.pitch: What matters is the speech, not who is speaking.
stations.spread: Justice Rehnquist dissents that the traits that make corporations useful in business could pose special dangers in politics.

stations.title: A law firm for the idea
stations.who: Chip Mellor and Clint Bolick; Charles Koch
stations.where: Institute for Justice, a libertarian public interest law firm
stations.what: Founded with Koch seed money of up to $500,000 a year for three years.
stations.pitch: Win liberty in court, one case at a time.
stations.spread: Files a brief for Citizens United and is co-counsel in SpeechNow.org v. FEC, the case that creates super PACs.

stations.title: Unfree Speech
stations.where: Unfree Speech: The Folly of Campaign Finance Reform (Princeton University Press)
stations.what: A book arguing that campaign finance limits do more harm than good.
stations.pitch: There is little proof that money corrupts politics, and reform makes things worse.
stations.spread: Smith serves on and chairs the FEC, then founds the Center for Competitive Politics in 2005.

stations.title: Close the loopholes
stations.who: Sens. John McCain and Russ Feingold; Congress
stations.what: Restricts corporate-funded ads that name candidates close to an election.
stations.pitch: Stop corporate money from coming in through the side door.
stations.spread: In 2008 the law blocks Hillary: The Movie. The fight over that film becomes Citizens United.

stations.title: A group to end the limits
stations.where: Center for Competitive Politics, now the Institute for Free Speech
stations.what: A group founded to fight contribution and spending limits.
stations.pitch: Political speech should be free of limits.
stations.spread: Co-counsel with the Institute for Justice in SpeechNow.org v. FEC.

stations.title: The test case
stations.who: David Bossie, Citizens United; lawyer James Bopp Jr.
stations.what: A film attacking Hillary Clinton is barred as campaign advertising under McCain-Feingold. Citizens United sues and loses.
stations.pitch: A documentary is not a campaign ad.
stations.spread: Ted Olson replaces Bopp at the Supreme Court and frames it as a First Amendment case.

stations.title: No limit on corporate spending
stations.who: Justice Anthony Kennedy, for a 5 to 4 Court
stations.what: Corporations and unions may spend without limit on independent political ads.
stations.pitch: The government may not limit political speech because the speaker is a corporation.
stations.spread: Cato and the Institute for Justice file briefs for Citizens United; Senators McCain and Feingold file for the FEC.

stations.title: The super PAC is born
stations.who: David Keating, SpeechNow.org; the Institute for Justice and the Center for Competitive Politics
stations.what: Groups that only spend independently may raise unlimited money.
stations.pitch: If independent spending cannot corrupt, neither can giving to it.
stations.spread: The Supreme Court declines to review. Groups modeled on SpeechNow multiply.

stations.title: The first big machine
stations.where: American Crossroads (super PAC) and Crossroads GPS (nonprofit)
stations.what: A super PAC paired with a nonprofit that mostly keeps its donors secret.
stations.pitch: Use the new rules before anyone else does.
stations.spread: $123 million raised through 2011, 62 percent of it through the secret-donor arm.

stations.title: No cap on a donor’s total
stations.who: Shaun McCutcheon and the RNC; Chief Justice John Roberts
stations.what: Strikes down the cap on how much one donor can give in total across candidates and parties.
stations.pitch: A cap on total giving is a cap on speech.
stations.spread: The biggest donors can give to as many candidates and committees as they like.

stations.title: Where it landed
stations.what: Harris for President raises and spends $1.175 billion. Trump’s main committee raises $496 million and spends $472 million.
stations.spread: Harris outspends Trump about two and a half to one on campaign committees, and loses. Outside super PACs, including Elon Musk’s, narrow the gap.

findings.title: The idea came first
findings.text: Winter’s argument for the American Enterprise Institute came in 1971, before the post-Watergate limits it attacked. It took the courts 39 years to get from there to the super PAC.

findings.title: Left and right together
findings.text: Buckley’s plaintiffs ran from Eugene McCarthy, the antiwar Democrat, and the Socialist Workers Party to the American Conservative Union.

findings.title: The money followed
findings.text: Presidential campaigns first passed $1 billion in 2008, by the FEC’s count, and spent $4.1 billion in 2020. That is the candidates alone, before super PACs.

counterpoints.claim: Spending money is how political speech reaches people. Citizens United began with a documentary about a candidate that the law barred from being shown.
Super PACs must disclose their donors. The secret money runs through nonprofits like Crossroads GPS, which is a disclosure problem, not a super PAC problem.
counterpoints.who: Center for Public Integrity reporting on Crossroads

counterpoints.claim: Money does not simply buy elections. In 2024 Harris’s campaign outspent Trump’s about two and a half to one, and lost.

About $15.1 billion in 2020 and $8.9 billion in the 2022 midterms. OpenSecrets projected at least $15.9 billion for 2024, with outside groups on track to pass $5 billion.
